newsitem.title: ITALY: Bosnian Fed wants Brcko deal based on 1991 census.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Fed wants Brcko deal based on 1991 census.

text.p: Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation wants a deal on the status of the disputed northern town of Brcko to be based on a 1991 census, when most of the population was Moslem or Croat, Vice-President Ejup Ganic said on Friday.
An Italian Foreign Ministry statement said Ganic made the remarks at a meeting with deputy foreign minister Piero Fassino in Rome, where international arbitration on the dispute opened this week.
Bosnian Serb leaders said on Thursday that any decision to award Brcko to the federation could lead to another war.

"(Ganic) expressed the hope that the question of jurisdiction over Brcko be resolved on the basis of data from the 1991 census, when the majority of the population resident in the area was ethnically Moslem or Croat," the statement said.
"Ganic underlined that the solution must guarantee full freedom of movement to all citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina."
The 1991 census was the last in the republic before war broke out among Serbs, Moslems and Croats, radically redrawing Bosnia's ethnic map.
The three-member arbitration panel has until February 15 to settle the status of Brcko, a strategic town which links Bosnian Serb territory to the west and east.
Biljana Plavsic, president of Bosnia's Serb republic, said on Thursday that Brcko was a Serb town and any change to that status would again invoke "the spectre of war in this area".
The arbitration session was expected to last until Saturday and to end with a decision to meet again in a so-far unspecified location. No one involved would comment on progress so far.

Lawyers representing the two sides were expected to present evidence to the arbitration panel, comprising chairman Roberts Owen, a U.S. lawyer, Cazim Sadikovic of the Moslem-Croat federation and Vitomir Popovic from the Bosnian Serb republic.

The narrow Brcko corridor, which straddles the Sava river border, is considered the most likely flashpoint in Bosnia, but the Dayton peace accord which ended Bosnia's 43-month Bosnian war failed to resolve the status of the town itself.
The federation says that allowing the Serbs to keep control of the town they seized early in the 1992-95 conflict would reward "ethnic cleansing" and violence.
